criteria.description: Identifies that SVD provides explicit orthonormal bases for input and output spaces, unlike raw (possibly dependent, non-orthogonal) rows/columns.
Identifies that SVD makes explicit which input direction maps to which output direction and by how much (singular values).

commonErrors: Only saying 'SVD decomposes a matrix' without explaining what specifically becomes clearer or easier as a result.
Confusing orthonormality of U/V with A itself being orthogonal (A is generally not orthogonal; only U and V are).

solutions.fullSolution: A raw matrix's rows/columns may be linearly dependent and are generally not orthonormal, so there's no explicit, clean basis describing the input or output space. The SVD A=USV^T provides exactly that: V's columns are an orthonormal basis for the input space, U's columns an orthonormal basis for the output space, and S's diagonal entries (singular values) tell you exactly how much each input basis direction gets scaled on its way to the corresponding output basis direction. Because the v_i are mutually orthogonal and the u_i are mutually orthogonal, A's whole action decomposes into k independent, non-interfering pieces: project onto v_i, scale by sigma_i, place along u_i, which is much easier to reason about than the raw matrix entries.

criteria.description: Correctly expands A^T A = V S^T U^T U S V^T and uses U^T U = I to simplify.
Correctly identifies S^T S = S^2 (diagonal matrix of squared singular values).
Correctly concludes A^T A = V S^2 V^T is the eigendecomposition, identifying V's columns as eigenvectors and sigma_i^2 as eigenvalues.

commonErrors: Forgetting to transpose correctly: (USV^T)^T = VS^T U^T, not USV^T again.
Not explicitly connecting the final form V S^2 V^T to the definition of an eigendecomposition (orthonormal eigenvector matrix times diagonal eigenvalue matrix times its transpose).

solutions.fullSolution:
A^T A = (USV^T)^T (USV^T) = V S^T U^T U S V^T. Since U is orthonormal, U^T U = I, so this becomes V S^T S V^T. Since S is diagonal, S^T S = S^2, the diagonal matrix of squared singular values. So A^T A = V S^2 V^T.

This is exactly the form of an eigendecomposition (orthonormal matrix, diagonal matrix, transpose of the same orthonormal matrix), so V's columns are orthonormal eigenvectors of A^T A, with eigenvalues sigma_i^2 (the diagonal entries of S^2). Practically: to compute an SVD by hand, find the eigendecomposition of A^T A to get V and the singular values (as square roots of the eigenvalues), then find U similarly from A A^T (or via U = AV S^-1).

A^T A = [[2,1],[0,2]] @ [[2,0],[1,2]] = [[5,2],[2,4]]. Eigenvalues of a symmetric [[p,q],[q,r]] matrix: (p+r)/2 +- sqrt(((p-r)/2)^2 + q^2). Here p=5, r=4, q=2: (9)/2 +- sqrt(0.25+4) = 4.5 +- sqrt(4.25) = 4.5 +- 2.0616. Eigenvalues: 6.5616 and 2.4384. Larger singular value = sqrt(6.5616) = 2.562 (verified independently with NumPy while authoring this module, matching to full precision).

criteria.description: Correctly derives (A^T A)^-1 = V S^-2 V^T from the SVD.
Correctly simplifies (A^T A)^-1 A^T using V^T V = I to arrive at V S^-1 U^T.
Correctly computes A^dagger A = I_n using U^T U = I.

commonErrors: Confusing V^T V (= I_n for full column rank) with V V^T (only = I_n if V is square, i.e. also full row rank).

solutions.fullSolution:
(A^T A)^-1 = (V S^2 V^T)^-1 = V S^-2 V^T (inverse of a similarity transform, valid since S is invertible for full column rank).
(A^T A)^-1 A^T = V S^-2 V^T (V S U^T) = V S^-2 (V^T V) S U^T = V S^-2 S U^T (using V^T V=I_n) = V S^-1 U^T = A^dagger. Matches.
A^dagger A = (V S^-1 U^T)(U S V^T) = V S^-1 (U^T U) S V^T = V S^-1 S V^T (using U^T U=I) = V V^T = I_n (using full column rank, V is n x n orthonormal so VV^T=I_n). (Numerically verified for a random 5x3 full-column-rank matrix while authoring this module: matched np.linalg.pinv to floating-point precision.)

criteria.description: Correctly shows every column of u v^T is a scalar multiple of u, hence a 1-dimensional column space (rank 1).
Explains why this makes rank-1 matrices the minimal/atomic building blocks: any rank-k matrix decomposes into exactly k such pieces via its SVD, no fewer would suffice.

commonErrors: Confusing rank 1 with 'small' or 'simple looking' rather than the precise column-space-dimension definition.
Not connecting back to why the SVD specifically (as opposed to an arbitrary decomposition) gives a minimal/canonical rank-1 decomposition.

solutions.fullSolution:
For a rank-1 matrix uv^T, column j is (uv^T)_{:,j} = v_j * u, i.e. every column is some scalar multiple of the single vector u. So the column space is spanned by u alone: 1-dimensional, i.e. rank 1.

The SVD sum A = sum_i sigma_i u_i v_i^T expresses A's entire action as k independent rank-1 pieces added together, each one an isolated input-direction-to-output-direction mapping. Since a rank-k matrix requires at least k rank-1 pieces to express as a sum (rank is subadditive: rank of a sum is at most the sum of ranks, so you can't do it with fewer than k rank-1 terms), and the SVD achieves exactly k, rank-1 matrices are literally the minimal, atomic units that any linear map decomposes into: nothing simpler than 'pick up one input direction, scale, place along one output direction' can capture a genuine directional mapping at all.

criteria.description: Correctly substitutes the eigendecomposition to get d^T C d = sum_i lambda_i c_i^2 with c_i=v_i^T d.
Correctly notes sum_i c_i^2 = 1 from d being a unit vector and {v_i} orthonormal.
Correctly argues the weighted average is maximized by putting all weight on lambda_1, with equality exactly at d=+-v_1.

commonErrors: Forgetting to justify why sum c_i^2=1 (this follows from d unit length + orthonormality of the v_i, it's not automatic from any decomposition).

solutions.fullSolution:
d^T C d = d^T (sum_i lambda_i v_i v_i^T) d = sum_i lambda_i (v_i^T d)^2 = sum_i lambda_i c_i^2 where c_i = v_i^T d.
Since {v_i} is an orthonormal basis and d has unit norm, sum_i c_i^2 = ||d||^2 = 1 (Parseval/orthonormal-coordinate identity).
So d^T C d = sum_i lambda_i c_i^2 is a weighted average of the eigenvalues lambda_i with non-negative weights c_i^2 summing to 1. Since lambda_1 is the largest, sum_i lambda_i c_i^2 <= lambda_1 sum_i c_i^2 = lambda_1, with equality iff all the weight sits on lambda_1, i.e. c_1=+-1 and c_i=0 for i>1, i.e. d=+-v_1. So the variance-maximizing direction is exactly the top eigenvector, with maximal variance lambda_1.

criteria.description: Correctly proves the <= direction (all eigenvalues non-negative implies PSD) via the eigendecomposition sum.
Correctly proves the => direction (PSD implies eigenvalues non-negative) by applying the PSD condition to an eigenvector itself.

commonErrors: Only proving one direction and treating the proof as complete (this is an iff, both directions are required).
In the forward direction, forgetting that ||h_j||^2 > 0 is what lets you divide/conclude lambda_j >= 0 (eigenvectors are nonzero by definition).

solutions.fullSolution:
(<=) Suppose all eigenvalues lambda_i >= 0. Using M = sum_i lambda_i h_i h_i^T: for any v, v^T M v = sum_i lambda_i (h_i^T v)^2. Each term is a non-negative number (lambda_i>=0) times a square (>=0), so the sum is >=0. Hence M is PSD.
(=>) Suppose M is PSD. Let h_j be any eigenvector, Mh_j = lambda_j h_j. Apply the PSD condition at v=h_j: h_j^T M h_j >= 0. But h_j^T M h_j = h_j^T (lambda_j h_j) = lambda_j ||h_j||^2. Since h_j != 0 (eigenvectors are nonzero by definition), ||h_j||^2 > 0, so lambda_j = (h_j^T M h_j)/||h_j||^2 >= 0. Since h_j was an arbitrary eigenvector, every eigenvalue is non-negative.

criteria.description: Correctly proves (a) by induction.
Correctly proves (b) by direct substitution.
Correctly proves (c) by computing v^T A w two ways and using symmetry of A.

commonErrors: In (c), forgetting to use A^T=A explicitly, without which the two computations of v^T A w wouldn't actually have to agree.

solutions.fullSolution:
(a) Induction on k. Base case k=1: A^1 v = A v = lambda v, given. Inductive step: assume A^(k-1) v = lambda^(k-1) v. Then A^k v = A(A^(k-1) v) = A(lambda^(k-1) v) = lambda^(k-1) (A v) = lambda^(k-1) (lambda v) = lambda^k v.
(b) (A + alpha*I) v = Av + alpha*I*v = lambda*v + alpha*v = (lambda+alpha)*v.
(c) Compute v^T A w two ways. Way 1: v^T A w = v^T (mu*w) = mu (v^T w) (using Aw=mu*w). Way 2: v^T A w = (A^T v)^T w = (Av)^T w (using A^T=A, symmetry) = (lambda*v)^T w = lambda (v^T w). So mu(v^T w) = lambda(v^T w), i.e. (mu-lambda)(v^T w) = 0. Since lambda != mu, v^T w = 0.

criteria.description: Correctly expands A^k x0 in the eigenbasis, factoring out lambda_1^k.
Correctly argues (lambda_i/lambda_1)^k -> 0 for i>=2 since |lambda_1| is strictly largest.
Correctly concludes the normalized direction converges to h_1, and explains the role of a nonzero c_1.

commonErrors: Not explaining why c_1 != 0 matters (if c_1=0 exactly, the method converges to the second-largest eigenvector instead; this is why random initialization is used, to guarantee c_1 != 0 with probability 1).

solutions.fullSolution:
A^k x0 = A^k (sum_i c_i h_i) = sum_i c_i (A^k h_i) = sum_i c_i lambda_i^k h_i (using A^k h_i = lambda_i^k h_i from the previous exercise's part (a)).
Factor out lambda_1^k: A^k x0 = lambda_1^k [ c_1 h_1 + sum_{i>=2} c_i (lambda_i/lambda_1)^k h_i ].
Since |lambda_1| is strictly the largest magnitude, |lambda_i/lambda_1| < 1 for all i>=2, so (lambda_i/lambda_1)^k -> 0 as k->infinity. Therefore A^k x0 / lambda_1^k -> c_1 h_1, i.e. A^k x0 becomes dominated by the h_1 component, and after normalizing to unit length at each step, the direction converges to h_1 (up to sign flips from lambda_1^k's sign if lambda_1<0). This requires c_1 != 0 (i.e. x0 genuinely has a component along h_1), which a random initialization guarantees with probability 1.

criteria.description: Correctly shows (lambda_max*I - A) v_i = (lambda_max - lambda_i) v_i, same eigenvectors, shifted+flipped eigenvalues.
Correctly argues this makes A's smallest eigenvalue become the largest for the shifted matrix, so the ordinary power method (applied to it) finds A's smallest eigenvector.

commonErrors: Forgetting that this reasoning requires lambda_max to actually be A's true largest eigenvalue (found by the outer/first power method loop), not an arbitrary shift.

solutions.fullSolution:
Using (A+alpha*I)v=(lambda+alpha)v with alpha=-1 scaling appropriately (or directly): (lambda_max*I - A) v_i = lambda_max*v_i - A*v_i = lambda_max*v_i - lambda_i*v_i = (lambda_max-lambda_i)*v_i. So lambda_max*I-A has the same eigenvectors v_i as A, with eigenvalues lambda_max-lambda_i.
Since lambda_max is A's largest eigenvalue, lambda_max-lambda_i >= 0 for every i, and this quantity is maximized exactly when lambda_i is A's smallest eigenvalue (largest gap lambda_max-lambda_min). So the eigenvector that was smallest for A becomes the one with the LARGEST eigenvalue for (lambda_max*I-A). Running the ordinary power method on (lambda_max*I-A) therefore converges to exactly that eigenvector, i.e. A's smallest eigenvector, and A's smallest eigenvalue is recovered as lambda_max minus the converged eigenvalue of the shifted matrix. (Numerically verified for a random 4x4 PD matrix with known eigenvalues while authoring this module: recovered smallest eigenvalue matched the true value to floating-point precision.)
